issues.legal_issue: An appeal may be maintained without a copy of the decree when the appellant could not file one because the court failed to draw up the formal decree.
material_facts: A trial court varied the shares in an existing partition decree but did not prepare a formal decree recording the variation.
The appealing party could not file a copy of the decree and, despite obtaining time and applying to the trial court to prepare one, the trial court refused.
issues.conclusion: The appeal was maintainable despite the absence of a copy of the decree because the defect was not the appellant’s fault and resulted from the trial court’s failure to prepare the decree.
issues.legal_principle: Order XLI rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure ordinarily requires a copy of the decree to accompany the memorandum of appeal. Under Jagat Dhish Bhargava v. Jawahar Lal Bhargava, (1961) 2 SCR 918, the requirement is generally mandatory, but exceptional circumstances may permit an appeal without the copy. A party should not lose the right of appeal when the court’s failure to prepare the decree made filing a copy impossible.

predicates.appeal_from_share_variation_order: A party appealed an order varying shares previously specified in a decree.
predicates.formal_decree_not_prepared: The court that made the order did not prepare a formal decree recording it.
predicates.appellant_could_not_obtain_copy_despite_: The appellant tried to obtain the formal decree but could not do so because the court did not prepare it.

issues.definition: When a party appeals an order varying specified shares and cannot obtain the formal decree despite efforts because the court did not prepare it, the appeal may proceed without a copy of that decree.

issues.legal_issue: A court may pass a further preliminary decree in a partition suit to revise shares after an event occurring before the final decree, and an order resolving a dispute over that revision is appealable.
material_facts: A preliminary decree in a partition suit specified the parties’ shares.
Two parties died after that decree but before the final decree, giving rise to a dispute among the surviving parties about how their shares devolved.
The trial court decided the dispute and redistributed the shares, but did not draw up a fresh formal preliminary decree.
issues.conclusion: The trial court could pass a second preliminary decree revising the shares while the final decree remained unpassed. Its decision resolving the dispute and varying the shares was a decree in itself and was appealable.
issues.legal_principle: The Code of Civil Procedure does not prohibit more than one preliminary decree in a partition suit. While the suit remains pending before the final decree, the court may decide disputes arising from later events and revise the shares; a contested decision doing so is appealable. The Court approved Kasi v. Ramanathan Chettiar, [1947] 2 M.L.J. 523, Raja Peary Mohan v. Manohar, (1923) 27 Cal. W.N. 989, and Parshuram v. Hirabai, AIR 1957 Bom. 59, and overruled Bharat Indu v. Yakub Hasan, (1913) ILR 35 All. 159, Kedernath v. Pattu Lal, ILR [1954] Luck. 557, and Joti Parshad v. Ganeshi Lal, AIR 1961 Punj. 120.

rule.if: partition_suit_before_final_decree and later_event_requires_share_revision and surviving_parties_dispute_devolution and court_decides_dispute_and_varies_shares

predicates.partition_suit_before_final_decree: The proceeding is a partition suit in which the final decree has not yet been passed.
predicates.later_event_requires_share_revision: An event occurring after the preliminary decree requires the parties’ specified shares to be changed.
predicates.surviving_parties_dispute_devolution: The surviving parties dispute how a deceased party’s share devolves.
predicates.court_decides_dispute_and_varies_shares: The court resolves the dispute and changes the shares specified in the earlier preliminary decree.

issues.definition: In a partition suit still awaiting its final decree, a later event requiring a share revision, followed by a court’s resolution of a dispute over devolution and revision of shares, permits a further preliminary decree and makes that decision appealable.

issues.legal_issue: A Jain widow cannot sell as an absolute owner a share in ancestral property allotted to her on partition when no custom grants her an absolute interest in such property.
material_facts: The widow received a share of ancestral property under a preliminary partition decree.
She later purported to sell that share to one of the parties.
The applicable custom granting Agarwala Jain widows an absolute interest concerned self-acquired property, not ancestral property.
issues.conclusion: The widow held only a limited, widow’s estate in her share of the ancestral property and could not sell it as an absolute owner; the attempted sale did not transfer the share, which descended equally to the three surviving parties.
issues.legal_principle: Under Hindu law, absent a contrary custom, a Jain widow takes a limited interest similar to a widow’s estate. The custom proved among Agarwala Jains granting widows an absolute estate and power of alienation applied to the husband’s self-acquired property, not ancestral property. The Court treated the statement in Mulla’s Hindu Law, 13th edition, paragraph 616, as correct and explained that Tulsiram Khirchand v. Chunnilal Panchamsao Parwar, AIR 1938 Nag. 391, did not establish an absolute interest in ancestral property.

predicates.widow_holds_partition_share_in_ancestral: A widow received a share in ancestral property through a partition.
predicates.custom_does_not_grant_absolute_ancestral: No applicable custom gives the widow an absolute interest in the ancestral property she received.
predicates.widow_alienates_share_as_absolute_owner: The widow purports to transfer that share as though she owns it absolutely.

issues.definition: When a widow receives a share of ancestral property in a partition, no custom gives her an absolute interest in it, and she purports to transfer it as an absolute owner, the transfer does not convey the share.

issues.legal_issue: A will is proved genuine when the evidence of execution is supported by reliable witnesses and the surrounding circumstances are consistent with the testator’s intentions and competence.
material_facts: The will was supported by the evidence of an attesting witness whose testimony was not affected by the inconsistency in another attesting witness’s statements, as well as by the scribe and the beneficiary, who was present at execution.
The testator was about seventy when he executed the will, but lived for nearly seven more years and was not shown to have been mentally or physically incompetent.
The will was registered, and its disposition was consistent with the testator’s stated dissatisfaction with one son and appreciation of the beneficiary’s care and conduct.
issues.conclusion: The will was duly executed and genuine; the beneficiary’s participation in its execution did not undermine it in the circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed proof of due execution together with the circumstances bearing on genuineness, including the testimony of witnesses, the testator’s competence, the naturalness of the disposition, registration, and the testator’s survival for years after execution. No statutory provision or earlier case is relied on for this determination in the judgment.

rule.if: will_validity_challenged and execution_supported_by_reliable_evidence and testator_competent_at_execution and surrounding_circumstances_support_will

predicates.will_validity_challenged: A party to the proceeding challenges the genuineness of a will.
predicates.execution_supported_by_reliable_evidence: Reliable evidence from witnesses or other persons with knowledge supports that the testator executed the will.
predicates.testator_competent_at_execution: The testator was mentally and physically competent when the will was made.
predicates.surrounding_circumstances_support_will: The surrounding circumstances, including the disposition and the testator’s subsequent conduct or circumstances, support the will’s genuineness.

issues.definition: When a will is challenged but reliable evidence supports its execution, the testator was competent, and the surrounding circumstances support it, the will is proved genuine.

issues.legal_issue: A person may will away a share of joint family property after severance of status and specification of that person’s share.
material_facts: The partition suit had been filed before the father made the will, resulting in severance of status among the joint family members.
A preliminary decree had specified the members’ shares before the will was made.
The will bequeathed the father’s share in the ancestral property to the beneficiary.
issues.conclusion: The father was competent to will the share he had obtained in the joint family property after severance of status and specification of shares.
issues.legal_principle: Although a Hindu cannot ordinarily will away joint family property while it remains joint, severance of status and specification of shares make the testator’s share available for testamentary disposition. The judgment relied on no earlier case or statutory provision for this conclusion.

predicates.testamentary_disposition_of_joint_family: A testator purports to dispose by will of property that was joint family property.
predicates.status_severed_before_will: The joint family members’ status had been severed before the testator made the will.
predicates.testator_share_specified_before_will: The testator’s share in the property had been specified before the will was made.

issues.definition: When a testator wills property that was joint family property after status has been severed and the testator’s share has been specified, the testator may dispose of that share by will.
